article.overview:
A surface navigation network demonstrator is a test of whether positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) can be provided to users on the lunar surface by a set of ground-based stations, possibly combined with signals from lunar-orbit satellites or Earth navigation satellites. Surface users such as landers, rovers, hoppers and astronauts need to know where they are and what time it is. The Moon has no GPS-like constellation of its own, and the Moon's curvature limits how far orbital signals reach the surface, which is why ground stations are studied as a complement to orbiters [13].

No surface navigation network has yet been flown as a complete system. The evidence in this article has different statuses: LuGRE, a GNSS receiver that flew on Firefly's Blue Ghost lander in 2025 and acquired and tracked Earth navigation signals on the lunar surface [1][2] (flown); Nokia's lunar cellular equipment on Intuitive Machines' IM-2 lander, which ran for about 25 minutes after the lander tipped over [5][9][11] (flown, communications rather than navigation); the ESA NAVISP Lunar Surface PNT Beacon / Moon Station developed by Qascom with OHB Italia, which reached an elegant breadboard demonstrator stage in the laboratory [3][4] (ground-tested design, not flown); and Lunar Pathfinder, ESA's first lunar relay satellite, intended to carry a navigation experiment and to be the precursor to the Moonlight service [6] (planned, orbital).
article.description:
A surface navigation network, as the term is used in this article, combines three kinds of element. The space segment consists of satellites in lunar orbit, or Earth navigation satellites (GPS and Galileo are the examples tested so far), that transmit ranging signals. The surface segment consists of fixed or mobile stations on the ground. A fixed station has a known location, so it can generate its own ranging signals and measure the errors in signals from orbit. The user segment consists of landers, rovers, hoppers, habitats and astronauts with receivers that combine the signals they hear to estimate position, velocity and time.

A demonstrator is an early test of some or all of these elements, usually with a small number of units, to show that the technology works in the real environment before it is relied upon. The catalogue name is generic. The sources reviewed do not define a single standard surface navigation network demonstrator hardware item, so the examples below show different parts of the same idea.

Two wider programmes provide context. NASA's LunaNet is described as a services network of interconnected nodes, with navigation broadcast and PNT services among the planned services [7]. ESA's Moonlight initiative begins with Lunar Pathfinder and is planned to add further satellites and, later, beacons on the surface [6][8]. Neither programme's surface element had a confirmed flight schedule in the sources accessed.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
**Demonstrating GNSS-based navigation at the Moon.** LuGRE tested whether GPS and Galileo signals can be acquired and tracked at lunar distances and on the surface, and whether they can support autonomous position, velocity and time determination [1][2]. The NAVISP beacon work and the LuGRE results both bear on whether surface users can rely on Earth-based signals or need a dedicated lunar system.

**Improving positioning accuracy with differential corrections.** A fixed station at a known location can compare the ranges it measures to satellites with the ranges that should be measured. The difference, or error, can be broadcast to nearby users, who subtract it from their own measurements. The Qascom design computes and broadcasts such corrections [4]. This is a general satellite-navigation technique; the sources reviewed did not use it to describe a flown lunar system.

**Supporting future surface operations.** Navigation and tracking matter for landing, launch and tracking the locations of mobile assets. NASA identifies surface positioning as a stated need for LunaNet [7].

**Monitoring the navigation system itself.** The Qascom station is also designed to collect satellite observables from the surface to support monitoring of the lunar communication and navigation system [4].
article.operating_principle:
Three operating principles appear in the sources.

**Earth GNSS reception at the Moon (LuGRE).** The receiver tracks radio signals from GPS and Galileo satellites on L1 and L5 frequencies. It measures pseudorange, carrier phase and Doppler, and uses them to estimate position, velocity and time [1][2]. Lunar reception is difficult because the receiver sees a limited number of satellites above its horizon and because the signals arrive very weak. LuGRE used a high-gain 3x3 planar antenna pointed towards Earth [1].

**Fixed surface beacon with differential corrections (NAVISP Moon Station).** The station generates ranging signals for nearby users. It collects observables from lunar navigation satellites, computes corrections and broadcasts them to users, who apply them to improve their own position estimates [4]. The sources report a correction validity window of several minutes for static and mobile users, without further explanation [4].

**Cellular-style local network (Nokia equipment on IM-2).** An LTE base station with integrated core network functions is mounted on the lander. User equipment on a surface vehicle connects to it through RF antennas. The network carried data between the vehicle and the lander, and telemetry back to Earth [5][9]. This is a communication network, not a navigation system, and it is included as a precedent for surface network infrastructure.
article.scientific_importance:
Navigation on the Moon is an enabling capability. Without it, surface assets cannot reliably know where they are relative to each other or to their intended targets, and the timing needed for communications and data correlation is harder to maintain. The LuGRE results are important because NASA describes them as the first demonstration to acquire and track Earth-based navigation signals on the lunar surface [2], and the peer-reviewed paper provides measured flight data [1]. The same paper reports that measured GPS L1 signal strength was lower than the pre-flight simulation. The authors say the root cause is under investigation and should not be read as inherent to lunar GNSS reception [1].

The NAVISP demonstrator matters as a test of the differential-correction approach. Its stated benefit depends on the scenario: a February 2026 Qascom presentation reported limited advantage in a moving-user scenario when the digital elevation model and differential corrections are used [4][10].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a surface navigation network. The examples are different types of system with different statuses. Their values are not directly comparable and no comparison table is given.

examples.name: ESA NAVISP Lunar Surface PNT Beacon / Moon Station (Qascom with OHB Italia)
examples.type: Ground-tested design; fixed surface beacon and differential reference station
examples.flight_status: Not flown. Elegant breadboard demonstrator deployed in the ESTEC navigation laboratory; preliminary flight-model design delivered [3][4].
examples.developers: Qascom, with OHB Italia; funded under ESA NAVISP Element 1 [3][4].
examples.technology_readiness_level: The NAVISP objective description states an elegant breadboard at TRL 4 [3]. The InsideGNSS summary does not state a TRL [4].
examples.mass_status: Design figure for a south-pole deployment, approximately 180 kg; not a measured value [4][10].
examples.dimensions_status: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.power_status: Design figure: approximately 440 W peak; not a measured value [4][10].
examples.payload_content: Lunar communication and navigation system receiver, configurable navigation beacon transmitter, and communication links to lunar users, lunar navigation satellites and Earth [4].
examples.performance: Meter-level positioning accuracy is quoted from simulation, not hardware measurement [4]. Moonlight architecture accuracy targets are 10 m for rovers, 50 m for landers and 100 m for orbiters [8]; these are targets, not measured results.
examples.text: The Moon Station is a fixed surface beacon. It generates ranging signals for nearby lunar users, computes and broadcasts differential corrections, and collects satellite observables from the surface to support monitoring of the lunar communication and navigation system [4]. The source describes it as designed for deployment near the lunar south pole; this is a design condition, and this article does not recommend any landing site.

examples.name: LuGRE, Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (flown on Blue Ghost, 2025)
examples.flight_status: Flown. Launched 15 January 2025 06:11 UTC; landed on the Moon 2 March 2025 08:34 UTC; payload power loss 16 March 2025 22:50 UTC [1].
examples.developers: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Agenzia Spaziale Italiana (ASI), Qascom and Politecnico di Torino; NASA SCaN programme provided funding and oversight [1][2].
examples.mass_status: Less than 5 kg for the flight model [1]; no exact value is published.
examples.dimensions_status: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.receiver: Two cold-redundant Qascom QN400-SPACE modules (RXA primary, RXB secondary), multi-frequency and multi-constellation, with a Xilinx Zynq 7000 SoC and an Analog Devices AD9361 RF front end [1].
examples.antenna: Passive 3x3 planar L-band array, right-hand circularly polarised; peak boresight gain 15.35 dBic at L1/E1 (12 degree half-power beamwidth) and 14.56 dBic at L5/E5 (16 degree) [1].
examples.measured_results: GPS and Galileo signals tracked on L1 and L5. Longest tracked signal (Galileo PRN 11) at about 433,220 km; fix at about 398,350 km on 16 March 2025 [1]. First surface navigation fix at 06:51:35 UTC on 3 March 2025 at about 356,237 km from Earth's surface, using GPS PRN 18 and 25 and Galileo PRN 2 and 34 (four satellites, eight signals) [1]. NASA's release describes the same surface acquisition as 2 a.m. EST on 3 March 2025 at about 225,000 miles [2]; the paper figures are quoted here.
examples.signal_strength_result: Measured GPS L1 C/N0 generally 7 to 12 dB below the pre-flight simulation; root cause under investigation and possibly within the integrated lander and payload system [1].
examples.operating_time: More than 111 hours of operation in total, more than 106 hours in tracking mode; more than 95 hours of surface operation, of which nearly 93 hours were real-time tracking [1].
examples.thermal_limits_recorded: Receiver peak 72 C; low-noise amplifier peak 68 C; high-gain antenna peak 115 C. Surface operations paused during lunar-noon heating [1].
examples.antenna_pointing: Required pointing within 1 degree of Earth's centre; achieved off-pointing under 0.73 degrees in transit and under 0.21 degrees on the surface [1].

examples.text: LuGRE is the first payload in this article with a flight record on the lunar surface. Its surface fix and tracking results come from the peer-reviewed paper [1] and from NASA's release [2]. The paper's extracted text did not include the signal-availability figures, navigation estimation results or position accuracy for the surface fix; these may appear in the full paper.

examples.name: Nokia cellular network on Intuitive Machines IM-2 (flown, 2025; communications, not navigation)
examples.flight_status: Flown on IM-2 Athena. Landed 6 March 2025 and tipped onto its side [5][11].
examples.architecture: LTE base station with integrated Evolved Packet Core functions, LTE user equipment, RF antennas and operations and maintenance control software. The user equipment was to be carried on Lunar Outpost's MAPP rover [9].
examples.mass_power_status: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.operation: Converge Digest reports that the system briefly operated within a narrow 25-minute power window after the tip-over reduced available solar power, and transmitted telemetry to Earth [5]. No data volume or link statistics are given in the sources accessed.
examples.limitation: The planned first cellular call on the lunar surface could not be established because severe temperature drops affected the Micro-Nova hopper module [5].
examples.text: This is the only example in the article that flew a surface network, and it did not provide navigation. Its operation was limited by the lander's attitude and solar power after landing [5][11].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are publicly specified for none of the three examples in the sources accessed. The Qascom design has no published envelope in the sources reviewed, LuGRE's dimensions are not stated in the paper, and the Nokia surface equipment's dimensions are not publicly specified. Any future station would need dimensions set by its mounting, thermal, antenna and deployment requirements.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The flight-model LuGRE receiver is stated as less than 5 kg [1]. The Qascom Moon Station is a design figure of approximately 180 kg for a south-pole deployment [4][10]. The Nokia surface equipment mass is not publicly specified. Mass drives launch and landing requirements, so these values are not interchangeable.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LuGRE maximum operational power is 14 W [1]. The Qascom Moon Station design peak power is approximately 440 W [4][10]. The Nokia surface equipment power is not publicly specified. The Qascom value is a design figure, not a measurement.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
The lunar surface has no substantial atmosphere, large temperature swings between lunar day and night, and exposure to radiation and micrometeoroids. The Qascom design notes that temperatures can fall below -150 C and that survival, active and operative modes were defined to get through the lunar day-night cycle [4]. The LuGRE flight data show that the receiver and antenna reached high temperatures during the lunar day, that surface operations were paused during lunar-noon heating, and that receiver clock stability tracked temperature [1].

A fixed beacon must be stable, because its known position is the reference for all corrections. Any movement of the station, or error in its surveyed position, propagates into every correction it broadcasts. The sources do not give a surveyed-position accuracy requirement.

Antenna pointing also matters. LuGRE's antenna needed to point within 1 degree of Earth's centre, and measured off-pointing was under 0.73 degrees in transit and under 0.21 degrees on the surface [1].
article.limitations:
**Signal availability.** A receiver on the lunar surface sees a limited set of Earth navigation satellites. In LuGRE, lower-than-predicted signal strength pushed many side-lobe signals below the acquisition threshold, which reduced availability and increased noise [1].

**Coverage and geometry.** A single station covers a limited area. The Qascom analysis gives coverage areas spanning hundreds of kilometres, based on simulation [4]. The orbital geometry for surface users is not fully characterised in the sources accessed.

**Benefit of differential corrections.** The Qascom presentation reports limited benefit in a moving-user scenario [4][10].

**Dependence on lunar reference systems.** LunaNet PNT service delivery depends on a defined lunar geodetic system and lunar time [7]. These definitions were not confirmed as final in the sources accessed.

**Schedule uncertainty.** The UNOOSA/ICG presentation of June 2024 gave an initial PNT service target of 2025 to 2026 [7]. No current programme update confirming this was found in the sources accessed.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface navigation station could be delivered to the Moon as a dedicated payload, as a hosted payload on a lander, or as part of a larger surface experiment package. LuGRE was delivered as one of several payloads on Firefly's Blue Ghost lander. Lunar Pathfinder is an orbital relay and navigation precursor, not a surface payload.
transportation_process: Integrate the payload into a lander or spacecraft on Earth, including its antenna and any thermal or power interfaces.
Launch on a launch vehicle, for example Falcon 9 for Blue Ghost missions [6].
Transfer to the Moon and enter lunar orbit or descend to the surface, depending on the mission profile.
Deliver the payload to the surface on a lander, or release it from an orbiter where that is the mission design.
Deploy, level and thermally protect any fixed station, then connect power, data and antenna interfaces.
Commission and verify signal reception, including Earth navigation signal acquisition, before science or service operations.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LuGRE operated as a payload on the Blue Ghost lander and was operated from it [1][2]. The Qascom station's deployment method is not described in the sources accessed. The Qascom design assumes deployment near the lunar south pole [4]; this article does not recommend any landing site. ESA's 2022 sensor-station briefing suggested, as a next step, either an in-space demonstration or a hosted payload on the European Large Logistics Lander [13].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LuGRE flew on Firefly's Blue Ghost lander, which touched down on 2 March 2025 [1][2]. The Nokia equipment flew on Intuitive Machines' IM-2 lander, which landed on 6 March 2025 and tipped onto its side [5][11]. Lunar Pathfinder is planned to be carried to lunar orbit on Blue Ghost Mission 2 under a NASA-ESA barter agreement [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Lander compatibility has not been verified for any surface navigation system described in this article. A future station's compatibility would need to be assessed from its mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, deployment method, power, thermal and communications requirements against verified lander specifications. No compatibility is asserted here.

article.historical_significance:
NASA describes LuGRE as the first technology demonstration to acquire and track Earth-based navigation signals on the lunar surface [2]. It also set an altitude record, with GNSS signal acquisition at 209,900 miles from Earth on 21 January 2025, beyond the record previously held by NASA's Magnetospheric Multiscale mission [2]. The peer-reviewed paper confirms surface acquisition and tracking and describes an open data set released in October 2025 [1].

Nokia and Intuitive Machines reported the IM-2 equipment as the first cellular network on the Moon [9]. Its operation was very short and the tip-over limited available power, so its historical significance rests on a brief demonstration rather than sustained use [5][11].

The NAVISP Moon Station is significant as a European ground demonstration of a surface beacon and differential reference concept, prepared to work with future lunar navigation orbiters [3][4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
**Scope of the category.** The catalogue entry is generic. This article does not claim that a single surface navigation network has been demonstrated. The examples have different statuses and should not be compared as if they were the same system.

**Flight versus ground status.** Only LuGRE has flown a navigation receiver to the lunar surface. The NAVISP Moon Station is a ground-tested design, and its mass and power are design figures, not measurements.

**Measured versus target.** Moonlight accuracy values of 10, 50 and 100 m are targets [8]. The meter-level accuracy for the Moon Station is from simulation [4]. Neither is a measured result.

**Source conflicts.** The LuGRE surface fix time and distance differ between the NASA release and the paper [1][2]. The Nokia operating time is described only as a 25-minute power window in a trade-press report [5]. The Lunar Pathfinder launch date differs between ESA's 2024 page and later secondary sources [6][12].

**Missing values.** Dimensions for the Moon Station and LuGRE are not stated in the sources accessed. Mass and power for the Nokia surface equipment are not publicly specified. LuGRE surface position accuracy and signal-availability figures may appear in the full paper but were not in the extracted text [1].

**Secondary sources.** Several claims rely on trade press or presentation summaries rather than full primary documents, including the Qascom presentation results and the NAVISP final presentation summary [3][4][10]. These should be checked against the original ESA NAVISP final report before publication.

The ESA image URL is the legacy media asset path from the ESA page's source-file link with its download query parameter removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Images without a verified direct asset are not included.

data_quality_notes: Scope: the catalogue name is generic. No single surface navigation network has been flown as a complete system; the examples have different statuses (flown, ground-tested, planned) and must not be compared directly.

LuGRE surface fix time and distance differ between the NASA release (2 a.m. EST, about 225,000 miles) and the peer-reviewed paper (06:51:35 UTC, about 356,237 km). The paper values are used in the article.

LuGRE dimensions are not stated in the paper or the NASA release. Surface position accuracy and signal-availability figures were not in the extracted text of the paper, which was truncated before those sections.

The Qascom Moon Station mass (about 180 kg) and power (about 440 W) are design figures for a south-pole deployment, not measured values. Its meter-level accuracy is from simulation. No TRL is stated in the InsideGNSS summary; the NAVISP objective description gives TRL 4 for the elegant breadboard.
The Qascom 2026 moving-user finding is from a search summary of a presentation that was not fetched directly.
The NAVISP final presentation deck PDF returned HTTP 404 and the Bell Labs IM-2 update page returned HTTP 410; neither was used as a source for values.

Nokia IM-2 network: the 25-minute figure is a power window described in a trade-press report, not a measured operating duration. No data volume or link statistics are available. No mass, dimensions or power are publicly specified for the surface equipment.

Lunar Pathfinder launch date conflicts: ESA's page (25 November 2024) says no earlier than end of 2025; a secondary source reports no earlier than 2027. Confirm with ESA or SSTL before relying on either.
No lander compatibility is asserted for any system in this article. The Qascom south-pole deployment is a design assumption in the source and is not a landing-site recommendation.
Image rights: NASA and ESA images are listed with their stated credits. Reuse terms were not checked beyond the source pages; confirm before republication.
Images: the four direct image URLs were checked with HTTP 200 and image/jpeg or image/png responses, and each source page was reviewed for caption and credit. No other images were used.
